alembic.whatItIs: Alembic, a tool that records changes to a database's layout, such as adding a table or a column, and applies them in order, for Python projects.
goodAt: Keeping a database's table layout in step with the app as it changes
Applying the same layout changes to a test database and a live one
notGoodAt: Hosting the database itself; set up the database server separately.
alembic.example: When the team adds a phone number field to customer records, the tool applies that change to the database in order, so every copy matches.

altair.whatItIs: Altair, a Python library for drawing charts by saying which columns go on which axis, rather than placing each mark by hand.
goodAt: Bar, line and scatter charts straight from a table of data
Interactive charts inside a notebook
notGoodAt: Live dashboards for many viewers; use a dashboard tool for that.
altair.example: When the notebook has revenue per region, one short line of code turns it into a bar chart with labeled axes.

asgi-lifespan.whatItIs: A Python test helper that runs a web app's startup and shutdown steps, so tests use an app that is fully set up.
goodAt: Running a web app's startup code, such as opening a database connection, inside tests
Letting tests send requests to the app once its resources are ready
notGoodAt: Running a live app; it's a test helper, so the real server handles startup there.
asgi-lifespan.example: When a test starts, the helper opens the app's database connection first, then closes it again once the test finishes.

asyncpg.whatItIs: asyncpg, a library that lets Python programs read and write a PostgreSQL database, a system for storing records in tables, without pausing the program while they wait.
goodAt: Letting a Python service load and save records in PostgreSQL
Running several database reads at once inside one program
notGoodAt: Designing the tables themselves; use a database design tool.
asyncpg.example: When a customer opens their order history, the app asks the database for saved orders and keeps serving other people while it waits.

django.whatItIs: Django, a Python framework for building websites whose pages are made on the server, with a database layer, a ready-made admin area, forms and page templates included.
goodAt: Building a website where people sign in, fill in forms and see saved records
Giving staff an admin area to browse and edit the stored data
notGoodAt: Pages that update live without reloading; pair it with htmx or a JavaScript framework.
django.example: When someone submits a sign-up form with a missing email, the page comes back with the form still filled in and a note next to the empty field.

django-stubs.whatItIs: Type descriptions for Django and a plugin that lets mypy, a type checker, understand Django's models, settings and querysets.

django-stubs-ext.whatItIs: A small runtime helper from django-stubs that lets code write Django's generic classes with a type in brackets, such as a form for one model.

djangorestframework.whatItIs: Django REST framework, an add-on for Django that turns its stored records into a service other programs and apps talk to, sending and receiving data instead of web pages.
goodAt: Letting a phone app or website read and save records kept in Django
Checking incoming data and naming each field that is wrong
notGoodAt: Websites whose pages are made on the server; plain Django does that.
djangorestframework.example: When a phone app sends a new note without a title, the service answers with an error naming the title instead of saving it.

djangorestframework-stubs.whatItIs: Type descriptions for Django REST framework and a plugin that lets mypy, a type checker, understand its serializers and views.

djlint.whatItIs: djLint, a tool that checks and tidies the HTML page templates of Django and similar frameworks.
goodAt: Keeping page templates consistently indented and formatted
Flagging template mistakes such as missing attributes or unclosed tags
notGoodAt: Checking Python code; use Ruff for that.
djlint.example: When someone saves a template with uneven indentation, the check fails and the format command lines it up again.

drf-spectacular.whatItIs: drf-spectacular, a tool that writes a machine-readable description of a Django REST framework service (an OpenAPI file) listing every address, the data each accepts and what it returns.
goodAt: Giving other teams an exact, up-to-date list of what the service accepts
Generating client code for apps that call the service
notGoodAt: Services built without Django REST framework; each framework has its own tool.
drf-spectacular.example: When a developer renames a field, the regenerated file shows the change, so callers learn about it before it ships.

duckdb.whatItIs: DuckDB, a database that runs inside a Python program with no server, for asking questions of data files in SQL.
goodAt: Running SQL directly over Parquet and CSV files on a laptop
Fast totals, rankings and joins over millions of rows
notGoodAt: Many people saving changes at once; use a server database such as PostgreSQL.
duckdb.example: When someone asks which products earned the most last month, one SQL query over the saved files lists them in order.

fastapi.whatItIs: FastAPI, a Python toolkit for building the server side of a website or phone app, the part that answers each request it receives.
goodAt: Building a service that answers requests from a website or phone app
Rejecting requests with missing or wrong details before the main code runs
notGoodAt: Storing data by itself; connect a database separately.
fastapi.example: When a phone app sends an order with no quantity, the service sends back an error that names the missing field instead of saving the order.

greenlet.whatItIs: A Python library that SQLAlchemy, a database toolkit, needs to run its database calls without holding up the rest of the program.
goodAt: Letting a Python service use SQLAlchemy's asynchronous database calls
Letting other requests proceed while a database query is still running
notGoodAt: Calling it directly from your code; SQLAlchemy uses it behind the scenes.
greenlet.example: When a shopper opens a saved cart, the service asks the database for the items and keeps answering other visitors while it waits.

gunicorn.whatItIs: Gunicorn, a program that runs a Python website on a server and hands each incoming request to one of several copies of the app.
goodAt: Running a Django or Flask site in production
Restarting a crashed copy of the app while the others keep answering
notGoodAt: Serving secure HTTPS connections itself; put a proxy or load balancer in front.
gunicorn.example: When several visitors load pages at the same moment, each request goes to a free copy of the app, so nobody waits behind a slow page.

httpx.whatItIs: httpx, a Python library that lets a program send web requests to other services, either one at a time or in the background.
goodAt: Fetching data from outside web services
Running many web requests at once without waiting for each one
notGoodAt: Building a web service that others call; use a web framework instead.
httpx.example: When someone enters a street address, the app asks an outside mapping service to check it and waits for the answer.

hypothesis.whatItIs: Hypothesis, a Python testing library that invents many inputs for a test, including awkward ones a person wouldn't think of, and shrinks any failure to the simplest example.
goodAt: Checking a rule that holds for every input, like reading back what was written
Finding unusual inputs that crash code which handles text or numbers
notGoodAt: Checking one exact expected answer; a plain pytest example test is clearer.
hypothesis.example: For a date parser, it tries thousands of strange dates and reports the shortest one that breaks it.

marimo.whatItIs: marimo, a Python notebook for exploring data, saved as a plain Python file that reruns the affected cells whenever a value changes.
goodAt: Exploring data with tables and charts that stay in step with the code
Notebooks that can be reviewed, checked and run like any other Python file
notGoodAt: Long-running scheduled jobs; run those as a pipeline command instead.
marimo.example: When an analyst changes the date filter at the top, every table and chart below it updates to match without rerunning cells by hand.

mypy.whatItIs: mypy, a checker that reads the notes a Python project adds about what kind of data each value holds, and reports mismatches before the program runs.
goodAt: Finding places where data of one kind is used as another kind
Keeping a large Python project consistent as it changes
notGoodAt: Checking data that arrives while the program runs; use Pydantic for that.
mypy.example: When a developer passes a price as text where the code expects a number, the checker flags it before anyone runs the code.

polars.whatItIs: Polars, a fast Python library for working with tables of data, such as filtering rows, joining tables and adding up totals.
goodAt: Cleaning and summarizing tables with millions of rows on one computer
Reading and writing CSV and Parquet files with the column types spelled out
notGoodAt: Data spread across many machines; use a warehouse or Spark for that.
polars.example: When a month of sales exports arrives, the pipeline drops broken rows and totals revenue per region in seconds.

pyarrow.whatItIs: The Python version of Apache Arrow, a shared in-memory table format that lets data tools such as DuckDB and Polars hand tables to each other without copying.

pydantic.whatItIs: Pydantic, a Python library that checks incoming data, such as form fields or settings, against rules about what each value must look like.
goodAt: Checking that a request from a website has every field it needs
Converting incoming text into the right kinds of values
notGoodAt: Storing records; use a database for that.
pydantic.example: When a sign-up sends an age as the word ten instead of a number, it rejects the data and says which field is wrong.

pydantic-settings.whatItIs: An add-on for Pydantic that reads an app's settings, such as a database address, from the system it runs on, and checks that they are present and valid.
goodAt: Reading settings from the system the app runs on
Stopping startup early when a required setting is missing
notGoodAt: Storing passwords and keys; use a secrets manager.
pydantic-settings.example: Before the app starts, it checks that the database address is set, and stops with a clear message if it is missing.

pytest.whatItIs: pytest, a Python tool that runs automated tests, small checks that confirm the code still does what it should.
goodAt: Running Python tests, from checks on one function to checks on a whole feature
Sharing setup code between related tests
notGoodAt: Clicking through a website the way a visitor does; use a browser testing tool.
pytest.example: After a developer changes how orders are saved, the test run repeats the order checks and reports any that fail.

pytest-asyncio.whatItIs: Adds support for testing Python asynchronous functions with pytest.

pytest-cov.whatItIs: Adds a report showing how much of the Python code the pytest tests run.

pytest-django.whatItIs: A pytest plugin that sets up Django for tests and gives each test that asks for it a fresh test database.

pytest-randomly.whatItIs: Runs pytest tests in a shuffled order to catch tests that only pass in one order, and fixes random choices so failures can be repeated.

pytest-xdist.whatItIs: Runs pytest tests across several helper programs at the same time.

ruff.whatItIs: Ruff, a Python tool that checks code for likely mistakes and untidy style, and reformats it to one standard layout.
goodAt: Catching unused code and small mistakes before a person reviews it
Keeping formatting the same across a Python project
notGoodAt: Checking whether the program behaves correctly; run tests for that.
ruff.example: When a developer saves a file with a leftover line that nothing uses, the tool flags the line and fixes the spacing to match the project's standard.

sqlalchemy.whatItIs: SQLAlchemy, a Python library that lets a program describe its database tables as code and read or write records through that description.
goodAt: Reading and saving records in a database from Python
Writing database queries in Python rather than the database's own language
notGoodAt: Changing a database's layout over time; use a tool for that, such as Alembic.
sqlalchemy.example: When a shopper's cart is saved, the program writes it to the database through Python code, without writing database commands by hand.

structlog.whatItIs: structlog, a Python library that writes a program's activity log as labeled pieces of information, so each entry can be searched and sorted.
goodAt: Attaching the same details, such as a request number, to every log entry
Making activity logs searchable across a whole service
notGoodAt: Collecting or storing logs; set up a log service separately.
structlog.example: When a customer reports a problem, support staff can search the activity log by request number and see every step that request took.

twine.whatItIs: Checks that a built Python package's description and details will display correctly on PyPI, and uploads it there.

typer.whatItIs: Typer, a Python library for building command-line programs, where each command is a plain function and its options come from the function's parameters.
goodAt: Building a terminal command with subcommands, options and help text
Rejecting a mistyped option before the program does any work
notGoodAt: Full-screen terminal interfaces; use Textual for those.
typer.example: When someone types the wrong option, the tool stops, names the option it didn't recognize and points to the help text.

uvicorn.whatItIs: uvicorn, a server program that runs a Python web app so it can receive requests from browsers and phone apps.
goodAt: Running a Python web service that answers requests from websites or phone apps
Starting a local copy of an app to test it on one computer
notGoodAt: Deciding what the app does with a request; use a web framework such as FastAPI.
uvicorn.example: When a phone app asks for a user's order list, the server hands the request to the app's code and sends the reply back.

whitenoise.whatItIs: WhiteNoise, a Python library that lets a web app send its own stylesheets, scripts and images, compressed and cached, without a separate file server.
goodAt: Serving a Django site's stylesheets and images from the app itself
Letting browsers keep those files cached until they change
notGoodAt: Files people upload to the site; store those with a file storage service.
whitenoise.example: When a visitor opens a second page, the browser reuses the stylesheet it already downloaded instead of fetching it again.
